title: A composite block in shear
summary: Two materials, one interface: cut a cavity, fill it with a second Body, tie the two together, and predict the apparent shear stiffness before you solve for it.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: A sandwich panel: two steel face sheets around an aluminium core, sheared through its thickness. Wide and thin on purpose — a specimen this shape keeps the free edges far from the middle, which is what the theory at the end assumes.

steps.title: Units
steps.explain: Millimetres, kilonewtons, megapascals.

steps.title: The outer material, as one solid block
steps.explain: Build it as if it were solid steel end to end: 200 × 200 mm in plan, 30 mm thick. The cavity for the core comes next.

steps.title: Cut the cavity for the core
steps.explain: `geometry.subtract` cuts a shape out of an existing Body — here, the middle third of the thickness, all the way through in plan. `block` is left as two disconnected slabs, 10 mm each, with nothing directly joining them: whatever goes in the gap is the only thing that will.

steps.title: A second Body to fill it
steps.explain: `core` is its own Body, exactly the size and position of the cavity it fills. Nothing about `geometry.addBox` says the two touch — the Model, right now, is two solids that happen to share a surface, mechanically unrelated.

steps.title: The outer material
steps.explain: Steel.

steps.title: The core material
steps.explain: Aluminium — a different modulus, and a different Poisson's ratio. This is the first tutorial where that difference is the entire point.

steps.title: Assign steel to the outer Body
steps.explain: `material.assign` takes one Material and any number of Bodies — but never the reverse. Two Bodies, two separate assignments.

steps.title: Assign aluminium to the core
steps.explain: Now every Body has exactly one Material, which is all `solve.run` requires — it says nothing yet about whether the two Bodies are connected.

steps.title: Mesh both Bodies
steps.explain: One `mesh.set` call covers every Body in the Model with the same lattice. That does not tie them together — a shared mesh setting is not a shared node — it only means both Bodies are ready to be.

steps.title: Name the interface, from the mesh
steps.explain: `block`'s own auto-named faces cover its six outer sides; a cavity cut all the way through in plan, like this one, does not leave a clean auto-generated Set on a lattice mesh the way a simple box's faces do. `geometry.nameFace` names a face Set directly from a geometric rule instead — a plane, here — evaluated against the real mesh boundary, and re-evaluated after every remesh. This one is the lower slab's top face, at the bottom of the cavity.

steps.title: Name the other side of the interface
steps.explain: The upper slab's bottom face, at the top of the cavity. Its outward normal points the other way, so the plane's normal flips too.

steps.title: Fix the base
steps.explain: The very bottom of the lower slab, clamped in every direction — the datum the shear is measured against.

steps.title: Restrain the top out of the shear plane
steps.explain: The top face is free to move sideways — that is the whole point — but held to zero in the other two directions, so what follows is shear and not some mixture of shear and bending.

steps.title: Prescribe the shear, not a force
steps.explain: `constraint.prescribe` sets one displacement component to a chosen non-zero value on a Set — here, `ux` on the top face. 0.3 mm over a 30 mm thickness is 1 % engineering shear strain. Prescribing the displacement, rather than a force, is what makes "apparent stiffness" a single well-defined number to solve for: reaction over prescribed motion, not the other way around.

steps.title: What happens without a tie
steps.explain: Solving right now would fail: `core` touches `block` geometrically, but the two Bodies still have entirely separate degrees of freedom, and nothing built so far restrains `core` at all. The engine reports it plainly — `solve.not-positive-definite`, a non-positive pivot, suggesting `constraint.fix` — because as far as the stiffness matrix is concerned, `core` is a rigid body floating in space. A shared mesh setting was never a bond.

steps.title: Tie the lower interface
steps.explain: `contact.add` glues two face Sets: every node of `slave` is constrained to the point it projects onto in `master`, in every displacement component — no gap, no sliding, `kind: "bonded"` is the only kind there is today. It costs an ordinary static solve, not a contact search, because it is a linear constraint inside the same operator.

steps.title: Tie the upper interface
steps.explain: The same tie, at the top of the core. Both interfaces have to be tied — one bonded face still leaves the other end of the core free to peel away.

steps.title: One Step, five Constraints
steps.explain: The two supports, the prescribed shear, and both ties — a Step is just the list of what is active together.

steps.title: Solve it
steps.explain: The reaction on `shear` is the total force it took to impose that 0.3 mm — everything the theory below needs.

steps.title: The bounds, the answer, and why it is outside them
steps.explain: Predict the range, then see where the real, finite specimen actually lands.
steps.theory:
Shear modulus from the two elastic constants, $G = E / (2(1+\nu))$: $G_{\text{steel}} = 80.77\,\mathrm{GPa}$, $G_{\text{aluminium}} = 26.32\,\mathrm{GPa}$. The core is a third of the thickness, the two steel face sheets together the other two thirds ($f_{\text{steel}} = 2/3$, $f_{\text{core}} = 1/3$).

The layers are stacked *along the direction the shear stress has to travel*, so equilibrium demands the same shear stress pass through each one in turn — the **series (Reuss) bound**:
$$\frac{1}{G_{\text{series}}} = \frac{f_{\text{steel}}}{G_{\text{steel}}} + \frac{f_{\text{core}}}{G_{\text{aluminium}}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad G_{\text{series}} = 47.80\,\mathrm{GPa}$$
The other extreme, if the same two materials instead sat side by side sharing the same top-to-bottom motion, is the **parallel (Voigt) bound**:
$$G_{\text{parallel}} = f_{\text{steel}} G_{\text{steel}} + f_{\text{core}} G_{\text{aluminium}} = 62.62\,\mathrm{GPa}$$
Before solving, the honest prediction is "somewhere in $[47.80, 62.62]$ GPa, close to the series end, since this is a series arrangement."

Reading the reaction on `shear` back as $\tau/\gamma$ gives $G_{\text{apparent}} \approx 46.4\,\mathrm{GPa}$ at this mesh (46.1 GPa at half the element size — settled to within 1 %, so this is not a mesh artefact). That is *below* the series bound, not inside $[47.80, 62.62]$. It is not a wrong answer: Reuss and Voigt bound the effective modulus of an infinite, periodic composite, and this specimen is one layer of each material with four free edges, not an infinite stack. A free edge can only let a structure deform *more* than the idealised infinite one, never less — the same reasoning behind $K_t = 3$ holding only for an infinite plate in the Kirsch tutorials. Landing just under the series bound, rather than inside the textbook range, is what a real, finite specimen of a series composite is supposed to do.
